name: Bright Green
lede: Bright green is a description, not a historic name: on a screen it means the most intense green the display can show, and the swatch here sits almost exactly on pure screen green.

sections.title: A screen's green
sections.body:
The swatch #01FF07 is 0.1 units from pure screen green, #00FF00, in our measurements [1]. Its lightness is about 88 and its chroma about 119, a level of intensity that ISCC-NBS (1955) files as "vivid yellowish green" [1]. The nearest name in our teaching set is [[chartreuse]], 5.2 units away [1].

This exact value goes by many names in our library, within two units of one another: Electric Green, Fluorescent Green, Highlighter Green, Hot Green, Neon Green, Poison Green, Radioactive Green, Harlequin and RAL's Luminous Green [1]. Most describe glow, not pigment. St Clair calls [[lime]] a very bright green, originally the fruit and now usually much more luminous, even neon [2].

sections.title: Bright green in paint
sections.body:
Painters had to build their bright greens. Ball reports that Veronese's bright green, seen in his *Adoration of the Kings* (1573), was mixed from three pigments applied in two layers, and it was so much his trademark that the later synthetic emerald green was known in France as *vert Paul Véronèse* [3]. Ball calls emerald green an eighteenth-century pigment, whereas the Pigment Compendium has it in use from about 1830, so the books disagree on the date [3][4]. For [[painter:paolo-veronese|Veronese]], the effect came from layering, not from a single tube [3].

In Millais's *Ophelia* (1851–2), the bright greens were mixed from Prussian blue and chrome yellow, and the Pre-Raphaelites' critics found such greens "unripe enough to cause indigestion" [3].

Older greens were fragile. Verdigris is bright green or blue when fresh and has always been judged fugitive, and Cennino wrote that it is nice to the eye but does not last [4]. Finlay says Flemish painters locked it in with a preserving varnish, which is why the bright green skirt in van Eyck's *Arnolfini Marriage* (1434) survives [5]. [[gem:malachite|Malachite]] gave a bright green only if it was ground coarsely, since finer powder turned paler [6].

sections.title: Bright green off the screen
sections.body:
In 1787 George Washington chose a bright green for the dining room at his plantation house, finding it "grateful to the eye" and less likely to fade [5]. Among stones, the bright green grossular garnet called tsavorite, from Kenya's Tsavo National Park, is brighter than [[gem:emerald|emerald]] [7]. The bright green button stones of Zabargad Island in the Red Sea are [[gem:peridot|peridot]] [7].

Bright green can also be a trick of reflection. Albers observes that a white ceiling or roof eave near a lawn can look bright green, reflected from the grass [8]. Eckstut adds that the same bright green object looks much darker in low light than in daylight [9].

Latin already had a word for it: *vitreus*, light or bright green [10].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive of 23,781 has a color within four units of this swatch covering even one per cent of its canvas [11]. That describes this archive, not painting as a whole, and these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings [11]. Veronese's mixed bright green is a different thing from this swatch, and the archive shows how far apart screen green and painted green sit [11][3].
